eigen.gap: You have read the coefficients of the row equation of $A - \lambda I$ as the eigenvector twice, then got $(1,-1)$ from $4x + 4y = 0$ right; reading the vector off the equation needs one more unaided success on another day
eigen.note: This is the second time: earlier you read $(1,2)$ off $-x + 2y = 0$. Plug your vector back into the row equation before you write it down

review.prompt: Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue of the matrix with rows $(3,1)$ and $(1,3)$, and check each by multiplying.
points: Eigenvalues are the roots of $\lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 8$, so $4$ and $2$
Each eigenline is the kernel of $A - \lambda I$
For $4$ the row equation $-x + y = 0$ gives $(1,1)$; for $2$ the row equation $x + y = 0$ gives $(1,-1)$, not the coefficients $(1,1)$
Checks by computing $Av$ and comparing with $\lambda v$

diagonalization.title: Diagonalization
diagonalization.note: You worked out the right idea on your own: in the basis of eigenvectors, $A$ sends the coordinates $(s,t)$ to $(3s, t)$, so the matrix there is diagonal with the eigenvalues on the diagonal. You said you were not sure, so this needs to become solid. Writing the change of basis as matrices has not been taught yet.

review.prompt: Draws without replacement from a small population (e.g. 2 balls from an urn of 2 red, 3 blue): write the full distribution of the number of a given kind drawn, with reasons.
points: Accounts for no replacement: probabilities change after each draw, so not binomial
Gives each probability by counting $\binom{n}{k}$ selections or by sequential draws

review.prompt: Procedural: a fixed number $n$ of independent trials, each with the same success probability $p$; ask for the probability of exactly $k$ successes, with the reason for each factor. Use a fresh context each time.
points: Recognises $n$ independent trials with the same $p$, so $X \sim \text{Bin}(n,p)$
$\binom{n}{k}$ counts which $k$ of the $n$ trials are the successes
$p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$ is the probability of one specific arrangement, by independence
